This section presents the line-by-line computations underlying the headline findings reported in A4. Tables follow the same five-column structure: country, item, USD per standardised unit, per cent of consumer price, implied per cent of GDP. Where a cell contains a range or an estimate flagged with “\~”, the range reflects volume or price uncertainty discussed in section A3.

### A5.5 International benchmarks

For the comparable measures referenced in A4: OECD-average fuel excise USD 0.55 per litre on petrol, 30 to 50 per cent of pump price, 1.5 to 2.5 per cent of GDP; South Africa USD 0.20 to 0.25 per litre. WHO recommended tobacco excise at least 75 per cent of retail pack price; South Africa raises approximately 0.4 per cent of GDP from tobacco; EU approximately 0.6 per cent. OECD alcohol excise USD 15 to 40 per LPA on beer, USD 25 to 50 per LPA on spirits; OECD alcohol revenue 0.4 to 0.6 per cent of GDP. UK SDIL GBP 0.18 to 0.24 per litre (approximately USD 0.23 to 0.30) by sugar content; Mexico approximately USD 0.05 per litre flat; South Africa HPL ZAR 0.0221 per gram of sugar above 4g/100ml.

# Appendix A. The full diagnostics

Both diagnostics use the five-column structure described in section A3.3. The structure-and-differentiation column compresses three of the five fields. Rows are organised by the seven-category typology of section A3.2.

## A.2 Sierra Leone — Excise Act, 1982 as amended through the Finance Act, 2026

Sierra Leone's schedule sits in the First Schedule to the Excise Act, 1982. The Act is amended annually through the Finance Acts. The current legal position reflects the Finance Act, 2026, signed by President Bio on 29 December 2025, gazetted 7 January 2026, and effective from 1 January 2026. Note that some legacy lines remain quoted in Old Leones (Le) and have not yet been redenominated to New Leones (NLe); these are flagged in the recent-changes column.

# Appendix B. Recent changes, year by year

This appendix documents the year-by-year changes that produced the current law shown in Appendix A. For each country, it begins with the starting position at the start of 2020 and tracks the substantive amendments in each Finance Act (Sierra Leone) or Excise Duty Amendment Act (Uganda) through to the most recent enacted instrument. Pending bills are flagged separately.

## B.2 Sierra Leone

### Starting position: at 1 January 2020 (post-FA2020)

Tobacco: 30% ad valorem on the wholesale price of cigarettes (introduced through the FA2018 reform) plus elevated import duties on all tobacco products. Alcohol: specific excise of USD 1.5/litre on alcoholic beverages of up to 10% ABV, USD 2/litre above 10% ABV — applied uniformly to imports and most domestic production. Soft drinks: energy drinks at 20%; excise also on bottled and processed water. Fuel: specific excise on petrol, diesel, kerosene, fuel oil and lubricating oils under tariff item 27.10 (rates inherited from earlier Finance Acts). FA2020 itself: added a single new line — imported fruit and vegetable juice at 20%. Telecommunications and financial services: not subject to excise duty under the 1982 Act. Telecom services within the GST net at 15%; financial services GST-exempt.

### Finance Act, 2021 (effective 1 January 2021)

- First major re-engineering of the alcohol regime. Tariff item 22.09 repealed and replaced with a four-band local-content beer regime: D1 (\>80% local) 5%; D2 (\>70%, \<80%) 8%; D3 (\>60%, \<70%) 12%; D4 (\>50%, \<60%) 15%.

- Eligible local raw materials defined as sorghum, cassava, maize, sugar and barley.

- Vegetable oils, palm olein and margarine added at 10% (heading 15.11).

- Soaps at 20% (heading 34.01).

- Industrial fatty-acid oils at 20% (heading 38.23).

- Nails at 5% (heading 73.17).

### Finance Act, 2022 (effective 1 January 2022)

No Schedule-level excise changes. The Act focused on income tax (cut petroleum operations from 30% to 25%), taxpayer segmentation, and digital-marketplace definitions in GST. Excise rates from FA2021 carried forward.

### Finance Act, 2023

Imposed a new set of regulatory levies on telecommunications operators (sometimes labelled “excise” colloquially but legally a separate levy under the Finance Act, not under the Excise Act): on-net mobile voice calls Le 0.1/minute; off-net Le 0.05/minute; outgoing international calls Le 0.2/minute; mobile money commissions 2%; mobile data up to 5% of recharge / bundle value.

### Finance Act, 2024 (effective 1 January 2024)

The most substantial single-Act re-write of the schedule in the period.

- Imported cement to 20%. Iron rod 10%. Cooking gas 5%. Rice graduated from 0 to 5% then 10% from 2025.

- Beer (heading 22.03) restructured: malt beer, stout, porter, non-alcoholic beer (≤5%) and “other” all at Le 0.01/cl or Le 10/litre local; Le 0.015/cl or Le 15/litre import.

- Wine (headings 22.04, 22.05) rebanded by ABV: Le 4.20/litre (≤10%), Le 6.30 (\>10–20%), Le 8.30 (\>20–30%), Le 10.40 (\>30–40%), Le 15.0 (\>40%) for local; Le 10/12/14/16/22/litre for imports along the same bands.

- Cigarettes restructured under tariff items 24.01–24.03 (specific tobacco rates per kg and per packet).

- Electronic cigarettes and cartridges introduced at item 24.04: Le 0.2/ml device, Le 0.4/unit cartridge.

- Fuel rates set at Le 0.81/litre kerosene, Le 2.80/litre petrol, Le 1.22/litre diesel rising on a published quarterly schedule to Le 2.40/litre by 1 October 2024, Le 4.14/litre fuel oil, Le 2.20/litre lubricating oils.

- Plastics: polyethylene bags and plastic bottles (with beverage, excluding water) at Le 16/kg.

- New excise on gambling, betting and lottery services at 10% of net wagered (gross gambling revenue less winnings) — inserted at item 98.01.

### Finance Act, 2025 (effective 1 January 2025)

First Finance Act in fully redenominated New Leone units. Two structural additions: section 5 (21-day excise payment rule) and section 48A (filing of excise returns with graduated penalties for large / medium / small taxpayers).

- Beer regime (item 22.09) re-tiered: D1 (\>80% local) at 5/8/12% across \<10, 10–20, ≥20 ABV; D2 (\>70–80%) at 8/12/15%; D3 (\>60–70%) at 12/15/17.5%; D4 (\>30–60%) at 15/17.5/20%. The local-content threshold for D4 widened from 50–60% to 30–60%, bringing more producers into the higher band.

- Tobacco (24.01–24.04) restated in NLe: unmanufactured tobacco NLe 65/kg; cigars and cigarillos NLe 25/packet; cigarettes NLe 2/packet of 20 sticks; other manufactured tobacco NLe 65/kg; shisha and herbal molasses NLe 65/kg + NLe 175/litre; e-cigarette device NLe 0.5/ml; cartridge NLe 0.8/unit.

### Finance Act, 2026 (effective 1 January 2026)

The latest enacted Finance Act. Tobacco and fuel re-tariffed upward, and cement re-stated.

- Cigarettes: rate raised to NLe 3/packet of 20 sticks (50% up from FA2025's NLe 2).

- Cigars / cigarillos: NLe 38/packet (up from NLe 25, \~52%).

- Unmanufactured tobacco / other manufactured tobacco: NLe 98/kg (up from NLe 65, \~51%).

- Shisha / hookah / vaping alternatives: NLe 98/kg + NLe 225/litre.

- E-cigarettes: NLe 0.75/ml device; NLe 1.20/unit cartridge (50% each).

- Cement (item 25.23): Portland, slag, super-sulphate and other hydraulic cement at NLe 10/50 kg bag.

- Fuel (item 27.10) restated in NLe: kerosene NLe 2/litre; petrol NLe 5/litre; diesel NLe 5/litre; fuel oil NLe 7.40/litre; lubricating oils NLe 4/litre.

- New annual circulation levy on vehicles (NLe 500 for ordinary cars / trucks / buses; USD 1,000 / 500 for large vessels and water taxis depending on capacity; NLe 200 for motorbikes), payable at importation, registration or licensing — structurally outside the Excise Act but fiscally adjacent.

**Commonalities with Uganda**

Read together, the two recent-changes histories show three common patterns. Both countries used the 2020 amendment cycle for selective COVID-related concessions and modest fuel-rate rises. Both used the 2021 amendment cycle to re-engineer the alcohol regime around local-content discounts. Both used the 2024 amendment cycle to broaden the base — Sierra Leone introducing e-cigarettes, gambling and plastic bottles; Uganda introducing payment services and powder-for-reconstitution-into-beer. Both have used the 2025 and 2026 cycles primarily for inflation catch-up — the cigarette-rate increases in both countries, the fuel restatements in Sierra Leone, the proposed fuel and motorcycle increases in Uganda's pending 2026 Bill.
